tasks.question: What does it mean for a t3 instance to be 'burstable', and what happens when its CPU credits run out?
options: A) t3 instances always run at full CPU speed with no limits — 'burstable' is just marketing language with no real effect

tasks.scenario: You proceed to resize reporting-db-01 from t3.micro to m5.large. Since EC2 doesn't support live/hot resizing, you stop the instance first. After changing the type and starting it back up, a colleague notices the temporary scratch files the nightly job used to write to /mnt/scratch are gone.
tasks.error_shown: ls: cannot access '/mnt/scratch': No such file or directory (the mount point that used to hold temporary query scratch space no longer has any data)
tasks.diagnosis: reporting-db-01 had an INSTANCE STORE volume (ephemeral storage, physically attached to the specific underlying host) mounted at /mnt/scratch, separate from its EBS-backed root volume. Instance store data is guaranteed to be wiped whenever an instance is stopped (or if it moves to different underlying hardware, which changing instance type causes) — this is expected, documented behavior, NOT a bug. The EBS-backed root volume (where the actual PostgreSQL data lived) persisted correctly through the stop/start, exactly as expected.
tasks.fix: This isn't something to "fix" — it's expected instance store behavior. If persistent scratch space is genuinely needed going forward, mount a small additional EBS volume at /mnt/scratch instead (EBS persists through stop/start and instance type changes; instance store does not). In this case, since it was only temporary query scratch space, nothing of real value was lost — but this is worth confirming explicitly rather than assuming.
tasks.explanation: This real, important distinction — EBS-backed root volume um instance store volume also different different behavior. Instance type change for doing stop must do, that instance store-ai WIPE does (guaranteed), but EBS volumes persist does. correct_answers.case_1: c5 (compute-optimized) — sustained high CPU usage fits a high CPU-to-memory ratio family, and being sustained (not bursty), a non-burstable family avoids any credit ceiling
